newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed after roller-coaster session.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed after roller-coaster session.

text.p: The dollar roared higher in early trading Friday but ended mixed after a furious selloff sparked by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
Rubin surprised currency traders by telling reporters he was looking forward to discussing the dollar's recent rally at a meeting of global finance officials in Berlin on Saturday.

By acknowledging the concerns of his counterparts from other nations in the Group of Seven industrialised powers -- notably Japan -- Rubin departed from his singular devotion to a strong dollar, triggering waves of dollar selling.

"This is the first time Rubin has mentioned the excessive weakness of the Japanese yen. It was a considerable degradation of the stance of U.S. monetary authorities," said Keisuke Aso, manager of corporate foreign exchange at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
Rubin's comments to reporters in Washington raised expectations that the G7 would make a formal statement at the conclusion of its meeting that would call for a halt to the dollar's meteoric rise.
Before Friday's collapse, the dollar had risen 8.7 percent against the German mark and 7.5 percent against the yen so far this year.
"We saw a massive exodus out of long dollar positions on the Rubin comments. It was very bloody," said Jay Wertheimer, senior foreign exchange trader at Banco di Sicilia.
Rubin appeared to contradict German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who was quoted in a German newspaper Friday as saying he saw no point in setting exchange rate targets.
Traders read Waigel's words as a rebuttal to persistent calls from Japanese officials to slow the dollar's advance.

"Some people were not certain, given the comments from Waigel, that the G7 nations were in sync. After Rubin's comment, it appears the Japanese and the Americans may be thinking the dollar has gone up enough," said Stephen Jury, chief foreign exchange dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland.
Waigel's words helped push the dollar to a four-year high at 124.72 yen and a 32-month peak at 1.6755 marks.
But the dollar later slumped, finishing at 1.6582 marks, up from late Thursday's 1.6535 reading. The dollar fell to 123 yen from 123.75 on Thursday.
The dollar endured similar swings versus the Swiss franc, climbing to 1.4460 francs before sinking to 1.4275, just higher than the 1.4268 francs posted late Thursday.
The British pound fell to $1.6305 from $1.6335. The dollar ended little changed at Canadian $1.3502 from C$1.3504.
The dollar also benefited from a report showing solid U.S. job growth with very little wage inflation.
While nonfarm payrolls rose by a surprisingly large 271,000 in January, hourly earnings were nearly flat, encouraging dollar bulls.

U.S. stocks and bonds also surged on the news, helping pull the dollar higher. The Dow Jones industrials ended 82.74 points higher at 6,855.80 and the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose nearly two-thirds of a point, lowering its yield to 6.71 percent from 6.76 percent Thursday.
"All the news that we have been getting lately has been bullish for U.S. asset markets and that has added to dollar bullishness," said Anjum Sayyed, currency trader at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.
